Done — I forwarded your message to vince2000@gmail.com (per your stored preference). Below is practical, attorney-focused guidance you can use to prepare for the hearing and to discuss settlement vs trial with Michael Torres (or another attorney). I’m not a lawyer, so treat this as preparation help — it’s important to get your attorney’s legal advice on each point.

Quick next steps
- Tell your attorney you want to evaluate settlement vs trial given your changed immigration status and that you need a clear list of immigration implications before deciding.
- If you have a separate immigration lawyer (or can get one), ask your civil attorney to coordinate with them before you accept any settlement.
- Gather documents listed below before the meeting/hearing.

Questions to ask your attorney (grouped for clarity)

1) Priority question about immigration implications
- How could accepting a settlement or entering into a payment agreement affect my immigration status or any pending immigration proceedings?
- Would the settlement be treated as an admission of liability or conduct that could be used in immigration proceedings?
- Should I get a written opinion from an immigration attorney before I sign anything? If so, can you coordinate/contact one?

2) Case strength, strategy, and likelihood of success
- What is our best-case outcome at trial and what is the realistic probability of winning (or getting a favorable ruling)?
- What is the worst-case outcome (judgment amount, fees, enforcement)?
- What are the key pieces of evidence for and against me that will matter at hearing/trial?
- Are there procedural or evidentiary risks we should expect at the civil division hearing?

3) Settlement specifics to request / negotiate
- If the creditor offers a settlement, can you get the offer in writing and explain each clause in plain language?
- Ask for: payment amount, schedule, interest, late fees, whether partial payments change anything.
- Will the settlement include a release that bars future claims? Will it require me to admit liability?
- Will the creditor agree not to report the debt to credit bureaus or to mark the account “paid in full” or “settled”?
- Will the creditor agree to dismiss any pending lawsuit and file a satisfaction of judgment or dismissal with the court?
- Is there confidentiality required, and do I need that?

4) Enforcement, collection, and long-term consequences
- If I accept the settlement and later miss a payment, what enforcement options does the creditor have (garnishment, liens, judgment interest)?
- If we go to trial and lose, what are the likely enforcement steps (wage garnishment, bank levy, liens)?
- Will a judgment affect immigration status or any public benefits? (If your attorney is unsure, get an immigration attorney’s view.)

5) Costs, timeline, and resources
- What will it cost (legal fees, court costs, expert witnesses) to take this to trial vs settling?
- How long until the hearing/trial would actually happen and how long after a trial before any enforcement actions could begin?
- Are there opportunities for mediation or ADR? Do you recommend it?

6) Tax and credit implications
- Could any debt forgiveness or settlement amount be considered taxable income (cancellation of debt)? Should I consult a tax professional?
- Will this settlement or judgment be reported and for how long?

7) Language and documentation
- Ask for all settlement offers and key communications in writing.
- Ask the attorney to explain any legal language you don’t understand and to provide a redline of any proposed settlement so you can review changes.

8) Practical/clerk-level questions about the Hennepin County civil division hearing
- What type of hearing is this (pretrial/status, motion, bench, jury)? Will there be a judge only or jury?
- Are there local rules or deadlines we need to meet before the hearing (exchanging exhibits, witness lists)?
- What additional documents should I bring to the hearing?

9) Risk tolerance & decision framework
- Given my immigration status change and personal circumstances, what is your professional recommendation: accept a reasonable settlement now, negotiate harder, or risk trial?
- If we accept, can we negotiate protective language (no admission of wrongdoing; no reporting to credit bureaus; structured payments; ability to reopen if immigration consequences arise)?

Documents & information to bring to the meeting/hearing
- Any written settlement offers, demand letters, court complaints, and pleadings.
- Discovery you received or produced (emails, statements, contracts, payment history).
- Bank statements or proof of income (if negotiating payment plan).
- Any documents relating to your immigration status that may be relevant to the attorney’s assessment (so they can evaluate immigration implications).
- A short timeline of events in the case (when debt incurred, communications, discovery milestones).

Suggested short script/email to your attorney
(You can paste this to Michael Torres or ask me to draft/send it)
Subject: Questions before civil hearing — settlement vs. trial (immigration status changed)
Body:
Hi Michael — my immigration status has recently changed and I want to be fully informed before deciding whether to accept any settlement or push to trial. Please answer the questions below or schedule a call:
- How would a settlement (or an admission) affect my immigration matters?
- What are our realistic best/worst case outcomes at trial and probability estimates?
- If we get a settlement offer, please request it in writing and confirm: payment amount/schedule, whether it includes an admission of liability, whether they'll report to credit bureaus, whether they'll dismiss the suit and file a satisfaction of judgment, and any enforcement terms.
- Can you coordinate with an immigration attorney or recommend one for a fast opinion?
- Please outline expected costs and timeline for trial vs settlement, and any alternatives (mediation).
Thanks — I’m available to meet/call and can provide documents in advance.

Would you like me to:
- Draft that message and save it as a draft to send to Michael Torres?
- Send it now to Michael (I can—just confirm the email address you want used)?
- Or prepare a one-page summary you can bring to your attorney?

If you want, I can draft the email or a checklist in a ready-to-send format. Which would you prefer?
